sets.title: What AI is and where it's going
What we know and what matters

statements.text: AI is better understood as a new kind of mind than as a tool or artifact.
Advanced AI poses a real risk of human extinction.
Technology-driven productivity growth leaves most workers better off even if public policy stays as it is.
Public promises about advanced AI are mostly inflated hype.
Market competition limits the harm that economic actors can do.
Over the next decade, AI will eliminate more jobs than it creates.
On its current course, advanced AI will concentrate wealth and power in a small number of companies.
AI-generated content is a serious threat to a society's shared sense of what is true.
How technology reshapes work and society is set by collective choices rather than by a fixed course of development.
AI should serve human beings as its end, and humanity should not be treated as a stage to be surpassed.
Public fear of AI exceeds what the evidence supports.
The AI dangers that most deserve attention come from how people deploy AI now, not from autonomous superintelligent agents.
AI systems may come to merit rights or moral consideration.
The history of earlier general-purpose technologies is a valid guide to how AI will behave and how people will receive it.
Political authority should rest on popular self-government rather than on experts, executives or other unelected powers.
On balance, market-driven technological development is good for people.
Most people would lose dignity and purpose without paid work, even if their income were fully replaced.
The leaders of major AI companies are being honest with the public about the risks of what they build.
Strict AI regulation now would do more harm than good, because it would deter innovation.
AI development should not be directed or controlled by the state.
Rivalry with China is a good reason for the United States to push ahead in advanced technology and keep its lead.
Distributing wealth or ownership directly to citizens is a sound way to share technology's gains.
Development of the most powerful general AI systems should be deliberately slowed or stopped.
AI companies should have to pay the people whose writing, art or data they train on.
Federal law should not prevent US states from passing their own AI laws.
As AI advances, people should receive a guaranteed income that is not tied to work.
The most capable AI models should be released openly for anyone to use and modify.

schools.label: AI as a new kind of risk
schools.note: They see a real risk of human extinction from advanced AI, want binding rules and early work on control, and don't think public fear of AI outruns the evidence.

children.label: Slow it down and govern it
children.note: They want the most powerful AI deliberately slowed and bound by government rules, because they don't trust companies to make it safe on their own.

children.label: Control work before it's needed
children.note: They don't think AI's promises are hype, see a real risk of extinction, and want serious work on control well before such systems exist; most oppose releasing the most capable models openly.

children.label: Extinction risk, shared gains
children.note: They all see a real risk of extinction; most back a guaranteed income not tied to work and sharing AI's gains directly with citizens, and don't think strict regulation would do more harm than good.

children.label: Ocasio-Cortez and Hoel
children.note: Closest here: AI's promises are mostly hype, the most powerful systems should be slowed and bound by government rules, and how technology reshapes society is a collective choice.

children.label: Altman and MacAskill
children.note: Closest here: AI's promises are not hype, the risk of extinction is real, and governments should impose binding rules on frontier developers.

schools.label: AI as a tool to govern
schools.note: They see AI as a tool rather than a new kind of mind, put today's harms ahead of superintelligence, and want binding rules because how technology changes society is a collective choice.

children.label: Doubt the hype, want binding rules
children.note: They see AI's promises as mostly hype, think that on its current course it will concentrate power in a few companies, and governments should impose binding rules on frontier developers.

children.label: Govern it like past technologies
children.note: They see AI as a tool rather than a new kind of mind, treat earlier technologies as a guide to it, and don't think its development should be kept out of the state's hands; most doubt a guaranteed income is the answer.

children.label: Shared truth and self-government
children.note: How technology reshapes society is a collective choice; most see AI-made content as a threat to shared truth, want technology to help diverse groups cooperate, and hold that political authority should rest with the public.

children.label: AI as an ordinary tool
children.note: They see AI as a tool rather than a new kind of mind, see no real risk of human extinction, think public promises about it are mostly hype, and put today's misuse ahead of superintelligence.

schools.label: Market optimists
schools.note: Public fear of AI outruns the evidence, market-driven technology is good for people, and strict regulation now would do more harm than good.

children.label: Let markets lead AI
children.note: Market-driven technology is good for people, public fear of AI outruns the evidence, and earlier technologies are a fair guide to it; most see no real risk of extinction and expect AI to create at least as many jobs as it cuts.

children.label: Progress as a choice
children.note: AI's promises are real, how technology reshapes society is a collective choice, market-driven technology is good for people, and strict regulation now would do more harm than good.

schools.label: Real promise, real risk, US lead
schools.note: They see both AI's promise and its risk of extinction as real, back keeping the US ahead of China, and want binding rules and early work on control; most think AI systems may come to merit moral consideration.

children.label: Superintelligence and a US lead
children.note: Closest here: autonomous superintelligence deserves at least as much attention as today's misuse, AI's promises are not hype, and most back keeping the US ahead of China.

notes: Thinkers are read by machine from about three public works each. None of them has reviewed this.
Agreement counts only statements where we found a stated position, never silence.
Schools are working labels made by clustering. The people named should replace them.
